analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour in steps and phases out the lower tipped wage.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee in July 2015 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage in five steps — $9, $10.50, $12, $13.50, then $15 an hour — and after five years would increase it automatically each year based on growth in the median hourly wage. It would also phase out the separate lower minimum wage for tipped workers, require employers to tell workers they may keep their tips, and let employers pay newly hired workers under 20 a reduced training wage for 90 days. It was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor issues and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning near the federal minimum wage, who would see raises on a set schedule reaching $15 an hour within about four years, plus tipped workers, whose base cash wage would climb until it matched the regular minimum wage.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in scheduled steps from $9.00 to $15.00 an hour over about four years [S2][S3].
After five years, the Secretary of Labor would raise the wage annually by the percentage increase in the median hourly wage of all employees, so it keeps pace with typical pay growth [S2][S3].

Phases out the separate, lower minimum wage for tipped employees, requiring tipped workers to eventually receive the full federal minimum from their employer, and requires employers to notify employees of their right to keep their tips [S2][S3].

Provides a youth training wage: employers may pay newly hired workers under 20 the minimum wage minus $3.00 for their first 90 days, and requires advance public notice (60 days) of each new wage level [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay at or near the current federal minimum — concentrated in food service, retail, and other low-wage industries — through higher labor costs, some of which may be passed to consumers as higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers like restaurants and retail

drawbacks.text: Businesses paying minimum wage would face sharply higher labor costs over four years, and critics argue some employers would respond by cutting hours, reducing hiring, automating, or raising prices [S3].

Full-service restaurants would absorb a double hit: higher minimum wages plus the elimination of the tipped-employee subminimum, which currently lets customers' tips cover part of the wage bill [S2][S3].
The bill applies one national wage floor across regions with very different costs of living, so the same $15 would be a larger change in low-wage, lower-cost areas than in high-cost cities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers paid near the minimum, the gains are direct and large — a raise to $15 in steps with automatic annual increases afterward. The costs fall on employers, concentrated in restaurants and retail, and economists disagree about how much of that shows up as fewer hours or jobs versus lower profits or slightly higher prices. The phase-out of the tipped minimum is the most contested piece, since it restructuring how servers are paid. The bill's design is straightforward and transparent: fixed steps, a published formula, and advance notice.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and nothing further — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on July 22, 2015, with Sen. Ed Markey, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S1][S3][S5].
The committee took no further action; the bill's complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral [S5].
The bill ended when the 114th Congress expired on January 3, 2017, without ever reaching the Senate floor or the House [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay minimum or near-minimum wages — especially restaurants and retail chains — avoided the higher wage costs the bill would have imposed, and the tipped-restaurant industry kept the existing lower wage for tipped workers.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the federal minimum wage to $15 and phase out the tipped minimum wage.

for.name: Sen. Ed Markey
for.what_they_did: Joined Sanders in introducing the bill.

for.name: 5 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it drew no Republican support.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: The Senate committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill; after referral on July 22, 2015, no action was ever taken on it.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate floor and committee agenda, 54 of 100 seats
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled Senate never scheduled it for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or independent; no Republican supported it, and with Republicans controlling the Senate and its committee agenda the bill never advanced past referral [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill raises the wage floor and eliminates the tipped subminimum, directly increasing restaurant labor costs. Tipped workers would gain a guaranteed full minimum wage from their employer; restaurant owners would pay more of their workers' pay directly.

Businesses that staff stores and operations at or near the federal minimum would face large scheduled cost increases through 2021 and automatic annual raises thereafter. Workers in these jobs would be the main beneficiaries.

Had it died, the bill's failure preserved the existing two-tier tipped wage system, in which employers may count customers' tips toward a large part of a server's required wage. Defeat kept that structure intact.
